deck.text: Six questions that separate genuine progress from headline figures

scenes.heading: Size is not capability
scenes.source: Our calculation, from the error rate per operation

notes.text: 1 in 100: a hundred steps run cleanly 37% of the time
1 in 1,000: ten thousand steps, once in 22,000 tries
1 in a million: the same steps, 99% of the time
Useful algorithms: millions to billions of operations

stats.label: error rate for the simplest useful applications
the best physical error rates today

items.text: Physical qubit: one device, such as an ion, an atom or a circuit
Logical qubit: information spread over many, by a code
Errors found and undone without disturbing it
Distance \(d\): physical errors needed for an undetected logical one
Surface code of distance \(d\): about \(2d^2\) physical qubits
Corrected over many rounds, or prepared and measured once?
Errors corrected, or only detected and the failed runs discarded?
Discarding wastes a fraction of runs that grows with the computation
Does it beat its parts? Google 2024: distance 7 outlived the best physical qubit by about 2.4×
Two-qubit gates: usually the weakest link
Measurement, idling, leakage and crosstalk errors count too
A headline fidelity is often the best pair on the chip
Randomized benchmarking: an average over many inputs
Coherent errors add up in step: the worst case can be far worse
What counts: how many operations fit in the coherence time

scenes.heading: Does the error fall as the code grows?

items.text: Below the threshold error rate: a larger code is more reliable
Above it: a larger code just collects more errors
Suppression factor \(\Lambda\): how much the logical error falls each time \(d\) grows by 2

scenes.heading: Compare slopes, not absolute values
scenes.source: Google Quantum AI, Nature 638 (2025); Lavasani et al., arXiv:2610.24077; extrapolation ours

notes.text: Google 2024, surface code: \(\Lambda\approx2.1\), error per round
Quantinuum 2026, colour code: \(\Lambda\approx12\), error per operation (preprint)
Billionfold: about 7,000 physical qubits per logical qubit, against about 900
Dashed lines are our extrapolation; correlated errors could break it

items.text: Logical gates between logical qubits
Including costly non-Clifford gates, usually supplied as magic states
Decoding fast enough to keep up during a long run

scenes.heading: Could a classical computer do the same?
scenes.source: Arute et al., Nature 574 (2019); IBM Research (2019); Pan, Chen and Zhang, PRL 129 (2022)

cells: 200 seconds on the processor; about 10,000 years on a supercomputer (their estimate)
About 2.5 days for an ideal classical simulation
About 15 hours on 512 GPUs, at the experiment's low fidelity

scenes.heading: Questions to ask
scenes.source: Cross et al., Phys. Rev. A 100, 032328 (2019): quantum volume

items.text: Was the classical baseline the best known method, and who proposed it?
Can the output be checked at all?
items.on: whether the output can be checked

items.text: A verifiable answer or a statistical certificate carries more weight
Quantum volume compares machines, but does not measure usefulness

scenes.heading: What would a useful task need?
scenes.source: Gidney, arXiv:2505.15917 (2025); Pappalardo et al., arXiv:2610.37839 (preprint)

cells: 0.1% gate error, 1 µs correction cycle, 10 µs reaction time
bit flips rarer than once a century per qubit; seconds are measured today

footer.text: Lower qubit counts usually rest on stronger assumptions

scenes.from: Speed matters as much as size
scenes.heading: Speed matters as much as size
scenes.source: J. Preskill, Beyond NISQ: The Megaquop Machine, arXiv:2502.17368 (2025)

items.text: Correction cycles a thousand times slower: one week becomes about two decades
A nearer milestone (Preskill): about a million operations run reliably
“Megaquop” machines: where correction starts to pay off, well before factoring

scenes.heading: Result, plan or product?
scenes.source: US Department of War (Quantum Benchmarking Initiative); US Department of Energy; Microsoft Quantum

items.text: Funders increasingly pay for verified performance
DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative: can any approach reach utility scale by 2033?
Utility: computational value above the machine's cost; hardware verified in the final stage
Department of Energy Q Competition: payments for lab-verified demonstrations of at least 100 logical qubits
Microsoft: judge reliability, scale, capability and performance together
